steps.title: Firm and dark
steps.body: Aglianico gives deep-coloured wines with high tannin and high acidity, a rare combination in a southern grape. Aromas include black cherry, plum, leather, tar, smoke and dried herbs. Its power and ageing potential have earned it the nickname the Barolo of the south.

steps.title: Ancient roots
steps.body: Aglianico has grown in southern Italy for centuries. Its name was once linked to Hellenic, suggesting a Greek origin, but DNA hasn't confirmed this, and the name may come from a Spanish-era word. It ripens very late, often in November, which lets it keep acidity even in a warm region.

steps.prompt: Why does Aglianico keep high acidity in the warm south of Italy?
options: It ripens very late, in cooler autumn weather, often at altitude
steps.explanation: Late ripening at altitude, into cool autumn nights, preserves acidity.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In the glass, Aglianico is dark ruby. On the nose, black cherry, plum, smoke and earth. On the palate, firm, sometimes rustic tannins, bright acidity and a long finish. Young wines can be severe; age brings leather, tobacco and dried fruit.

steps.prompt: Which aromas are typical of Aglianico?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Aglianico combines high tannin and high acidity
It ripens very late, keeping freshness in the south
It's called the Barolo of the south for its power and age
